Specifically: (1) phi = -0.478 (P = 0.000) tests state extension involvement on institutional rule choice (whether a community adopts a proportional per-livestock vs. flat numerical per-household fee rule), and phi = 0.155 (P = 0.244) tests solar/diesel pump technology on fee rule choice, both failing Criterion 4; (2) Table 1 (rbc = 0.559, P = 0.000; rbc = 0.427, P = 0.017; rbc = 0.406, P = 0.006; rbc = 0.389, P = 0.003) tests proportional vs. flat water tariff rules on four subjective social satisfaction ratings (rules, committee work, community cooperation, and general water management), which the authors explicitly characterize as social perception indicators rather than physical water supply/access; and (3) the distributional analysis of household water consumption shares and livestock wealth inequality under flat fees (Fig. 1) is a deterministic simulation model rather than an empirical inferential test. rationale: The full text (in Spanish, with English/Portuguese/French abstracts) empirically evaluates municipal cadastral updating (actualización catastral, mandated every 5 years under Colombia's Ley 1450 de 2011 Art. 24 and tied to property tax valuation and SSPD/SGP utility coverage certification under Ley 1176 de 2007 and Decreto 416 de 2007) across municipalities in Caldas, Quindío, and Risaralda. printed_headline_estimate: CWS reform vs matched IWS wards (SES-adjusted OLS, Table 4, PDF p. 7 / p. 126): Ongoing water expenditures = +111.679*** Rs/month (SE = 11.385, p < 0.01, N = 2,739; unadjusted CWS mean 204 [95% CI: 186.6–220.3] vs IWS 96 [95% CI: 81.9–111.2], Table 3); Amortized storage/coping investment = -133.644*** Rs/month (SE = 4.875, p < 0.01, N = 3,453; CWS 115 [95% CI: 109.6–120.4] vs IWS 251 [95% CI: 240.8–261.2]); Total monetary water costs = –32.633*** Rs/month (SE = 12.330, p < 0.01, N = 2,688; CWS 310 [95% CI: 292.5–327.5] vs IWS 354 [95% CI: 334.3–374.2]); Water waiting/management time = –22.632*** hours/month (SE = 0.683, p < 0.01, N = 3,078; CWS 7.4 [95% CI: 7.1–7.7] vs IWS 29.9 [95% CI: 28.5–31.2]). Affordability (Fig. 4, PDF p. 8): utility bills rose from >1% (IWS) to >3% (CWS) of reported income in bottom two wealth quintiles (non-overlapping 95% CIs; NS in top quintile); billed volumes increased significantly across all quintiles (Fig. 5). Secondary Family A covariate in Table 4 ('Own their Home'): +23.230* Rs/month on Total Monetary Costs (SE = 14.032, p < 0.10, N = 2,688), +13.173 (SE = 12.911, NS) on Ongoing Expenditures, and +0.193 hours/month (SE = 0.762, NS) on Time.
rationale: Using a genetic-matched quasi-experimental cohort of 3,922 enrolled households across 8 continuous water supply (CWS) demonstration wards and 8 intermittent water supply (IWS) control wards in Hubli-Dharwad, India (n = 1,969 CWS; n = 1,953 IWS), the paper reports 95% confidence intervals (Table 3, Figs. 2–5) and SES-adjusted OLS regressions (Table 4, N = 2,688 to 3,453) evaluating the KUWASIP municipal water system reform. Under KUWASIP (Family C: tariffs/administrative-structure/utility reform), all household connections were mandatorily registered with the utility, metered with a Rs 30/month meter fee plus an increasing-block volumetric tariff (replacing Rs 90 flat-rate / subsidized tariffs; Table 2), free public standpipes and borewells were decommissioned to eliminate non-revenue water, and pipes were upgraded to 24x7 continuous supply. The reform nearly doubled monthly ongoing water bill expenditures (+111.679*** Rs/month, p < 0.01) and significantly raised water bills as a share of income from >1% to >3% in the two poorest wealth quintiles (affordability outcome), while reducing total monthly monetary water costs once amortized storage investments are included (–32.633*** Rs/month, p < 0.01), cutting household waiting/collection time (–22.632*** hours/month, p < 0.01), and increasing billed water consumption across all quintiles. Confidence is set to medium because the CWS treatment indicator bundles the tariff, metering, registration, and public-tap-closure rules with physical pipe replacement and 24x7 hydraulic pressurization (the authors note they cannot separate tariff increases from higher consumption in the bill increase). Table 4 also reports inferential OLS estimates for household tenure ('Own their Home', Family A) on water expenditures and collection time.
